claim: Chronic autoimmune diseases are associated with mutations in PTPN22.
source: Chronic autoimmune diseases are associated with mutations in PTPN22, a modifier of T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about PTPN22 and autoimmune diseases.

claim: PTPN22 is a modifier of T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
source: Chronic autoimmune diseases are associated with mutations in PTPN22, a modifier of T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of PTPN22.

claim: The activity of PTPN22 is redox regulated.
source: As with all protein tyrosine phosphatases, the activity of PTPN22 is redox regulated, but if or how such regulation can modulate inflammatory pathways in vivo is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a property of PTPN22 shared with all protein tyrosine phosphatases.

claim: The C129 residue in PTPN22 is proposed to alter the redox regulatory properties of PTPN22 by forming a disulfide with the catalytic C227 residue.
source: To determine this, we created a mouse with a cysteine-to-serine mutation at position 129 in PTPN22 (C129S), a residue proposed to alter the redox regulatory properties of PTPN22 by forming a disulfide with the catalytic C227 residue.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the rationale for creating the C129S mutant mouse.

claim: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response.
source: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response and development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells, an effect neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1, a component of the NOX2 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The C129S mutant mouse showed development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis.
source: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response and development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells, an effect neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1, a component of the NOX2 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The enhanced inflammatory response in C129S mutant mice is due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells.
source: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response and development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells, an effect neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1, a component of the NOX2 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the mechanism underlying the observed phenotype.

claim: The effect of C129S mutation on inflammatory response is neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1.
source: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response and development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells, an effect neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1, a component of the NOX2 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ncf1 is a component of the NOX2 complex.
source: The C129S mutant mouse showed a stronger T-cell-dependent inflammatory response and development of T-cell-dependent autoimmune arthritis due to enhanced TCR signaling and activation of T cells, an effect neutralized by a mutation in Ncf1, a component of the NOX2 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about Ncf1.

claim: The C129S mutated PTPN22 protein has increased sensitivity to oxidation.
source: Activity assays with purified proteins suggest that the functional results can be explained by an increased sensitivity to oxidation of the C129S mutated PTPN22 protein.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro activity assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: The disulfide of native PTPN22 can be directly reduced by the thioredoxin system.
source: We also observed that the disulfide of native PTPN22 can be directly reduced by the thioredoxin system, while the C129S mutant lacking this disulfide was less amenable to reductive reactivation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro reactivation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The C129S mutant lacking the C129-C227 disulfide was less amenable to reductive reactivation.
source: We also observed that the disulfide of native PTPN22 can be directly reduced by the thioredoxin system, while the C129S mutant lacking this disulfide was less amenable to reductive reactivation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro reactivation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: PTPN22 functionally interacts with Ncf1.
source: In conclusion, we show that PTPN22 functionally interacts with Ncf1 and is regulated by oxidation via the noncatalytic C129 residue and oxidation-prone PTPN22 leads to increased severity in the development of T-cell-dependent autoimmunity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study, supported by the genetic interaction data.

claim: PTPN22 is regulated by oxidation via the noncatalytic C129 residue.
source: In conclusion, we show that PTPN22 functionally interacts with Ncf1 and is regulated by oxidation via the noncatalytic C129 residue and oxidation-prone PTPN22 leads to increased severity in the development of T-cell-dependent autoimmunity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study, supported by in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Oxidation-prone PTPN22 leads to increased severity in the development of T-cell-dependent autoimmunity.
source: In conclusion, we show that PTPN22 functionally interacts with Ncf1 and is regulated by oxidation via the noncatalytic C129 residue and oxidation-prone PTPN22 leads to increased severity in the development of T-cell-dependent autoimmunity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study, supported by the arthritis and DTH model data.

claim: Complex autoimmune diseases affect 4–5% of the human population.
source: Complex autoimmune diseases affect 4–5% of the human population, and large efforts have been invested in finding the underlying genetic polymorphisms (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the prevalence claim.

claim: A major genetic contribution to autoimmune diseases comes from the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region.
source: Though a major genetic contribution comes from the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region, many other loci have also been identified.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about autoimmune disease genetics.

claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in PTPN22 is associated with autoimmune diseases.
source: Two important single-nucleotide polymorphisms have emerged, one located in PTPN22 (Bottini et al., 2004), a cytoplasmic class I protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP), and the other in NCF1 (Olsson et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2017), a component of the NOX2 complex, controlling induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the association.

claim: PTPN22 is a cytoplasmic class I protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP).
source: Two important single-nucleotide polymorphisms have emerged, one located in PTPN22 (Bottini et al., 2004), a cytoplasmic class I protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP), and the other in NCF1 (Olsson et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2017), a component of the NOX2 complex, controlling induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of PTPN22.

claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in NCF1 is associated with autoimmune diseases.
source: Two important single-nucleotide polymorphisms have emerged, one located in PTPN22 (Bottini et al., 2004), a cytoplasmic class I protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP), and the other in NCF1 (Olsson et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2017), a component of the NOX2 complex, controlling induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the association.

claim: NCF1 controls induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in antigen-presenting cells.
source: Two important single-nucleotide polymorphisms have emerged, one located in PTPN22 (Bottini et al., 2004), a cytoplasmic class I protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP), and the other in NCF1 (Olsson et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2017), a component of the NOX2 complex, controlling induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in antigen-presenting cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of NCF1 function.

claim: Mutations in Ncf1 leading to a lower NOX2-dependent ROS response have been shown to be a major predisposing genetic factor for autoimmune diseases in both mice and humans.
source: Mutations in Ncf1, leading to a lower NOX2-dependent ROS response, have been shown to be a major predisposing genetic factor for autoimmune diseases in both mice and humans (Olsson et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: PTPN22 is primarily a dominant negative regulator of T cell responsiveness.
source: PTPN22 is primarily a dominant negative regulator of T cell responsiveness, acting by dephosphorylating important target proteins in the T cell signaling machinery, including LCK, FYN, and ZAP70 (Bottini and Peterson, 2014; Stanford and Bottini, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: PTPN22 acts by dephosphorylating important target proteins in the T cell signaling machinery, including LCK, FYN, and ZAP70.
source: PTPN22 is primarily a dominant negative regulator of T cell responsiveness, acting by dephosphorylating important target proteins in the T cell signaling machinery, including LCK, FYN, and ZAP70 (Bottini and Peterson, 2014; Stanford and Bottini, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Studies on PTPN22 have thus far focused on the effects of knocking out the gene or on the autoimmune variant Ptpn22R620W, but with divergent results.
source: Studies on PTPN22 have thus far focused on the effects of knocking out the gene or on the autoimmune variant Ptpn22R620W, but with divergent results (Carmona and Martín, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The activity of PTPN22 is dependent upon the integrity of a catalytic active site Cys residue.
source: Its activity is, as with other PTPs, dependent upon the integrity of a catalytic active site Cys residue.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a property of PTPN22 shared with other PTPs.

claim: The reactivity of the catalytic cysteine makes it particularly susceptible to oxidation via ROS, leading to concomitant abrogation of PTP activity.
source: The reactivity of this cysteine makes it particularly susceptible to oxidation via ROS, leading to concomitant abrogation of PTP activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a property of PTPs.

claim: Reversible oxidation and reduction of reactive cysteines has previously been shown to be a regulatory mechanism in signal transduction.
source: Reversible oxidation and reduction of such reactive cysteines has previously been shown to be a regulatory mechanism in signal transduction, regulating important T cell downstream signaling molecules such as NF-KB, NRF2, MAPK, and ERK (Kesarwani et al., 2013; Ostman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Control of redox regulation of PTPs in cells depends upon the balance between inhibitory oxidation of the catalytic Cys residue and its activation by reduction, where the latter is typically maintained by the thioredoxin system.
source: Control of redox regulation of PTPs in cells depends upon the balance between inhibitory oxidation of the catalytic Cys residue and its activation by reduction, where the latter is typically maintained by the thioredoxin system.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PTP regulation.

claim: The PTPN22 catalytic cysteine (C227) has been suggested to form a disulfide bond with another 'back-door' cysteine (C129), possibly altering the threshold for irreversible oxidation of C227 and thereby affecting the redox state of the active site.
source: Interestingly, the PTPN22 catalytic cysteine (C227) has been suggested to form a disulfide bond with another 'back-door' cysteine (C129), possibly altering the threshold for irreversible oxidation of C227 and thereby affecting the redox state of the active site (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mice with the C129S amino acid replacement developed increased T-cell-dependent inflammatory responses due to enhanced T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
source: We found that mice with this amino acid replacement developed increased T-cell-dependent inflammatory responses due to enhanced T cell receptor (TCR) signaling, which was dependent on NOX2-produced ROS.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the findings.

claim: The increased T-cell-dependent inflammatory responses in C129S mice was dependent on NOX2-produced ROS.
source: We found that mice with this amino acid replacement developed increased T-cell-dependent inflammatory responses due to enhanced T cell receptor (TCR) signaling, which was dependent on NOX2-produced ROS.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the findings.

claim: Recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S has a lower overall turnover compared to wild-type PTPN22.
source: This correlated well with findings of a lower overall turnover, higher sensitivity to inhibitory oxidation, and a lower capacity of reductive reactivation by the thioredoxin system of recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S compared to wild-type PTPN22.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the findings.

claim: Recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S has higher sensitivity to inhibitory oxidation compared to wild-type PTPN22.
source: This correlated well with findings of a lower overall turnover, higher sensitivity to inhibitory oxidation, and a lower capacity of reductive reactivation by the thioredoxin system of recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S compared to wild-type PTPN22.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the findings.

claim: Recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S has a lower capacity of reductive reactivation by the thioredoxin system compared to wild-type PTPN22.
source: This correlated well with findings of a lower overall turnover, higher sensitivity to inhibitory oxidation, and a lower capacity of reductive reactivation by the thioredoxin system of recombinant mutant PTPN22C129S compared to wild-type PTPN22.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the findings.

claim: Redox regulation of PTPN22 modulates inflammation in vivo.
source: These results show that redox regulation of PTPN22 modulates inflammation in vivo, with a lower resistance to oxidation of PTPN22 promoting aggravated disease.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the study.

claim: A lower resistance to oxidation of PTPN22 promotes aggravated disease.
source: These results show that redox regulation of PTPN22 modulates inflammation in vivo, with a lower resistance to oxidation of PTPN22 promoting aggravated disease.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Wild-type PTPN22 enzyme had a basal turnover of 19.6 min–1 with a Km of 4.57 mM.
source: wild-type PTPN22 enzyme had a basal turnover of 19.6 min–1 with a Km of 4.57 mM while PTPN22C129S displayed a turnover of 11.9 min–1 and a Km of 8.02 mM under the same conditions
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PTPN22C129S displayed a turnover of 11.9 min–1 and a Km of 8.02 mM.
source: wild-type PTPN22 enzyme had a basal turnover of 19.6 min–1 with a Km of 4.57 mM while PTPN22C129S displayed a turnover of 11.9 min–1 and a Km of 8.02 mM under the same conditions
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The C129S protein has retained PTP activity but with an overall lower catalytic efficiency.
source: showing that the C129S protein has retained PTP activity but with an overall lower catalytic efficiency (Figure 1A), which confirms Tsai et al.'s results (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A, with a citation to previous work.

claim: Addition of 50 µM H2O2 to pre-reduced wild-type PTPN22 led to inhibition of approximately half the activity after 20 min incubation.
source: We found that addition of 50 µM H2O2 to the pure protein led to inhibition of approximately half the activity after 20 min incubation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Addition of bicarbonate together with H2O2 noticeably potentiated the inactivation of PTPN22.
source: We also found that addition of bicarbonate together with H2O2 noticeably potentiated the inactivation (Figure 1C), similar to the properties shown earlier for PTP1B that are likely due to the formation of peroxymonocarbonate that reacts more efficiently than H2O2 with the PTP enzyme (Dagnell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C, with a citation to previous work on PTP1B.

claim: The mutant PTPN22C129S enzyme was clearly more sensitive to inhibition by H2O2 than wild-type PTPN22.
source: When comparing the H2O2 sensitivity of PTPN22C129S with that of wild-type PTPN22, we found that the mutant enzyme was clearly more sensitive to inhibition by H2O2 than wild-type PTPN22, although it had a lower basal turnover (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: H2O2-inactivated PTPN22 species could be reactivated in vitro using either DTT as reductant or the thioredoxin system composed of NADPH together with TrxR1 and Trx1.
source: We found that H2O2-inactivated PTPN22 species could be reactivated in vitro using either DTT as reductant or the thioredoxin system composed of NADPH together with TrxR1 and Trx1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Wild-type PTPN22, but not the PTPN22C129S mutant, could be directly reactivated by TrxR1 together with NADPH, without inclusion of Trx1.
source: Interestingly, wild-type PTPN22, but not the PTPN22C129S mutant, could be directly reactivated by TrxR1 together with NADPH, without inclusion of Trx1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The oxidized forms of wild-type PTPN22 were clearly more amenable to direct reactivation by TrxR1 than those of PTPN22C129S.
source: Subsequent experiments showed that the effect of TrxR1-dependent reactivation was concentration dependent and that the oxidized forms of wild-type PTPN22 were clearly more amenable to direct reactivation by TrxR1 than those of PTPN22C129S (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only PTPN22 but not PTPN22C129S displayed a second faster migrating form of the protein upon oxidation that disappeared upon reduction with DTT or TrxR1.
source: Indeed, only PTPN22 but not PTPN22C129S displayed a second faster migrating form of the protein upon oxidation that disappeared upon reduction with DTT or TrxR1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reactivation of wild-type PTPN22, with either DTT or the thioredoxin system (TrxR1 alone, or coupled with either Trx1 or TRP14), was always more efficient than that of the mutant PTPN22C129S enzyme.
source: We also found that the reactivation of wild-type PTPN22, with either DTT or the thioredoxin system (TrxR1 alone, or coupled with either Trx1 or TRP14), was always more efficient than that of the mutant PTPN22C129S enzyme, also in cases where prior oxidation was further potentiated by bicarbonate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased ear pinna thickness was observed in PTPN22C129S mice 24, 48, and 72 hr after challenge compared to littermate wild-type mice.
source: We observed increased ear pinna thickness in PTPN22C129S mice 24, 48, and 72 hr after challenge compared to littermate wild-type mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PTPN22C129S did not enhance ear swelling in NCF1 mutant mice with a lack of NOX2 activity.
source: In contrast, PTPN22C129S did not enhance ear swelling in NCF1 mutant mice with a lack of NOX2 activity (Figure 3C, Olofsson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C, with a citation.

claim: A marked increase in IFNɣ and IL-2-producing PTPN22C129S cells was observed when comparing wild-type supporting a Th1 phenotype.
source: To assess the antigen-specific T cell response, we restimulated cells from inguinal lymph nodes with the immunodominant COL2 peptide (259–273) and observed a marked increase in IFNɣ and IL-2-producing PTPN22C129S cells when comparing wild-type supporting a Th1 phenotype (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: No difference in IFNɣ and IL-2-producing cells was observed in the NCF1 mutant background.
source: No difference was observed in the NCF1 mutant background.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Higher CD4 expression was observed in COL2-injected PTPN22C129S ears compared to wild-type with no difference in the NCF1 mutants.
source: Additionally, we observed higher CD4 expression in COL2-injected PTPN22 ears compared to wild-type with no difference in the NCF1 mutants (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: qPCR analysis of the ears showed increased expression of CXCR3 in inflamed PTPN22C129S ears.
source: To further support the Th1 phenotype, we performed qPCR analysis of the ears that showed increased expression of CXCR3 in inflamed PTPN22C129S ears (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Immunized PTPN22C129S mice had increased cell numbers in the spleen compared to wild-type.
source: In the periphery, immunized PTPN22C129S mice had increased cell numbers in the spleen compared to wild-type (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Within the inguinal lymph nodes, a reduction in CD4+ T cells was observed, which expressed higher levels of CD44, a marker for effector-memory T cells.
source: Within the inguinal lymph nodes, we observed a reduction in CD4+ T cells, which expressed higher levels of CD44, a marker for effector-memory T cells (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J.

claim: There was a significant reduction in FOXP3+ T cells in PTPN22C129S mice 48 hr after initial immunization.
source: This was not seen in circulating T cells within the blood; however, there was a significant reduction in FOXP3+ T cells in PTPN22C129S mice 48 hr after initial immunization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTPN22C129S did not affect the expansion of antigen-specific Vβ12+ T cells per se.
source: Upon immunization with COL2, PTPN22C129S did not affect the expansion of antigen-specific Vβ12+ T cells per se (Figure 3K)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3K.

claim: PTPN22C129S changed the activation status of COL2-reactive T cells: they expressed higher levels of CD44 on CD4+ T cells compared to wild-type.
source: but did change their activation status: COL2-reactive T cells in the periphery expressed higher levels of CD44 on CD4+ T cells compared to wild-type (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Higher B22a1 expression was observed among CD4+ T cells in the inflamed ears of Vβ12.PTPN22C129S mice.
source: In the DTH model, we could also observe higher B22a1 expression among CD4+ T cells in the inflamed ears of Vβ12.PTPN22C129S mice (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Increased arthritis severity was observed in PTPN22C129S mice from day 10 up to day 22 after onset.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we observed increased arthritis severity in PTPN22C129S mice from day 10 up to day 22 after onset as well as increased incidence in mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increased incidence of arthritis was observed in PTPN22C129S mutant mice.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we observed increased arthritis severity in PTPN22C129S mice from day 10 up to day 22 after onset as well as increased incidence in mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: On the NCF1-deficient background, a trend in the opposite direction was observed with PTPN22C129S mice showing less disease and no significant difference in disease incidence.
source: On the NCF1-deficient background, we observed a trend in the opposite direction with PTPN22C129S mice showing less disease and no significant difference in disease incidence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PTPN22C129S mice showed higher antigen-specific T cell responses as shown by increased numbers of IFNɣ-secreting T cells, both upon GPIp and anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation.
source: Increased disease was further supported by higher antigen-specific T cell responses in PTPN22C129S mice as shown by increased numbers of IFNɣ-secreting T cells, both upon GPIp and anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD4 T cells in the draining lymph nodes exhibited increased activation as evidenced by higher numbers of CD4+ CD69+, CD4+ CD25+ FOXP3+ and CD4+ PD1+ T cells.
source: CD4 T cells in the draining lymph nodes exhibited increased activation as evidenced by higher numbers of CD4+ CD69+, CD4+ CD25+ FOXP3+ and CD4+ PD1+ T cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No differences were observed in serum antibody levels against the hGPI peptide.
source: No differences were observed in serum antibody levels against the hGPI peptide (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PTPN22 expression was comparable between wild-type, PTPN22C129S, NCF1m1J, and PTPN22C129S/NCF1m1J mice both via mRNA and protein analysis using splenocytes or sorted CD4+ T cells, respectively.
source: To understand where the observed T cell activation phenotype in PTPN22C129S mice originates from, we first confirmed that PTPN22 expression was comparable between wild-type, PTPN22C129S, NCF1m1J, and PTPN22C129S/NCF1m1J mice both via mRNA and protein analysis using splenocytes or sorted CD4+ T cells, respectively (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTPN22C129S was found to not affect immune cell populations in peripheral lymphoid organs in naïve mice.
source: Next, we analyzed expansion of naïve immune cell populations. PTPN22C129S was found to not affect immune cell populations in peripheral lymphoid organs in naïve mice; the percentages of B cells (B220+), T cells (CD3+), dendritic cells (CD11c+), and macrophages (CD11B+) were comparable to wild-type littermates as was MHC II expression on antigen-presenting cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A slight reduction in the percentage of CD4-CD8- (DN) population was observed in PTPN22C129S thymi.
source: We observed a slight reduction in the percentage of CD4-CD8- (DN) population whilst CD4+CD8+ (DP), CD4+, and CD8+ were comparable between groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Further fractionation of the early CD4-CD8- progenitor population showed a slight increase in DN1 (CD44+CD25-) and decrease in DN4 (CD44-CD25-) populations in PTPN22C129S thymi.
source: Further fractionation of the early CD4-CD8- progenitor population showed a slight increase in DN1 (CD44+CD25-) and decrease in DN4 (CD44-CD25-) populations in PTPN22C129S thymi (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No changes were observed in TCRb, CD5, and CD69 expression in PTPN22C129S thymi.
source: No changes were observed in TCRb, CD5, and CD69 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Percentages of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells as well as expression of CD44, and CD69 activation markers on CD4+ T cells were not affected by PTPN22C129S.
source: Percentages of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells as well as expression of CD44, and CD69 activation markers on CD4+ T cells were not affected (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Percentages of CD4+ FOXP3+ and CD4+ FOXP3+ CD25+ cells were comparable between groups in thymus and peripheral lymphoid organs.
source: Furthermore, percentages of CD4+ FOXP3+ and CD4+ FOXP3+ CD25+ cells were comparable between groups in thymus and peripheral lymphoid organs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Slightly increased intracellular Ca2+ was observed in PTPN22C129S CD4 T cells upon anti-CD3 stimulation.
source: To assess signaling, we measured Ca2+-flux, one of the earliest signaling events upon TCR engagement and observed slightly increased intracellular Ca2+ in PTPN22C129S CD4 T cells upon anti-CD3 stimulation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Proliferation of CD4 T cells was increased upon anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation in PTPN22C129S cells.
source: Proliferation of CD4 T cells, as assessed by CellTrace dilution, was also increased upon anti-CD3/anti-CD28 stimulation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Increased activation of ex vivo-stimulated CD4 T cells was observed as measured by the early T cell activation marker CD69.
source: We observed increased activation of ex vivo-stimulated CD4 T cells as measured by the early T cell activation marker CD69 as well as markedly different IFNɣ production resembling the in vivo results (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Markedly different IFNɣ production was observed in ex vivo-stimulated PTPN22C129S CD4 T cells resembling the in vivo results.
source: We observed increased activation of ex vivo-stimulated CD4 T cells as measured by the early T cell activation marker CD69 as well as markedly different IFNɣ production resembling the in vivo results (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: TCR stimulation of wild-type and mutant cells revealed increases in phosphorylation of tyrosines Y420 and Y394 of the Src family kinases Fyn and LCK, respectively, as well as of Y493 of Zap70.
source: TCR stimulation of wild-type and mutant cells revealed increases in phosphorylation of tyrosines Y420 and Y394 of the Src family kinases Fyn and LCK, respectively, as well as of Y493 of Zap70, thus agreeing well with lower intracellular phosphatase activity of the PTPN22C129S mutant protein (Figure 6A and B) and confirming findings with recombinant PTPN22 proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: PTPN22C129S lymph node cells showed constitutive phosphorylation of Y538 on PKC-θ, independent of TCR stimulation.
source: Compared to wild-type, PTPN22C129S lymph node cells showed constitutive phosphorylation of Y538 on PKC-θ, independent of TCR stimulation, whereas in wild-type cells phosphorylation increased with TCR stimulation, hinting at higher basal activity of PKC-θ in the mutant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Treatment with BSO initially reverted the phospho-PKC-θ levels in the mutant to be comparable with wild-type, followed by a slower TCR-activation-dependent phosphorylation.
source: Here, it initially reverted the phospho-PKC-θ levels in the mutant to be comparable with wild-type, followed by a slower TCR-activation-dependent phosphorylation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mass spectrometric proteomics analysis of activated cells revealed differential expression of multiple genes under both untreated and BSO-treated conditions.
source: Next, we investigated how differential signaling was affecting the proteome signature using sorted CD4+ T cells from wild-type and PTPN22C129S mice. Mass spectrometric proteomics analysis of activated cells revealed differential expression of multiple genes under both untreated and BSO-treated conditions: upregulation of Nudt16l1 (Baciu et al., 2000; Denhez et al., 2002), Clic4 (Suh et al., 2007), Mgmt (Boldogh et al., 1998), Hsp (Koliński et al., 2016), Serpina1e (Janciauskiene et al., 2017), and Fscn1 (Liu et al., 2016), as well as downregulation of Fuca1 (Vecchio et al., 2017) and Rps6kb1 (Romanelli et al., 1999), have all been shown to be associated with increased PKC signaling (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D, with citations for each gene's association with PKC signaling.

claim: The C129S mutation in Ptpn22 leads to reduced catalytic activity and increased susceptibility to oxidative inactivation in vitro.
source: In this study, we investigated whether redox regulation of PTPN22 has an impact on inflammation and autoimmune arthritis. We found that the C129S mutation in Ptpn22 leads to reduced catalytic activity and increased susceptibility to oxidative inactivation in vitro, causing concomitant upregulation of T cell activation and T-cell-mediated autoimmunity in a NOX2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The C129S mutation causes concomitant upregulation of T cell activation and T-cell-mediated autoimmunity in a NOX2-dependent manner.
source: In this study, we investigated whether redox regulation of PTPN22 has an impact on inflammation and autoimmune arthritis. We found that the C129S mutation in Ptpn22 leads to reduced catalytic activity and increased susceptibility to oxidative inactivation in vitro, causing concomitant upregulation of T cell activation and T-cell-mediated autoimmunity in a NOX2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Significant ROS producers include the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase (NOX) complexes as well as the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
source: Significant ROS producers include the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase (NOX) complexes as well as the mitochondrial respiratory chain, modulating responses such as cell growth, death, and immune function under both physiological and pathological conditions (Schieber and Chandel, 2014; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The protective effects of ROS against autoimmune diseases in vivo are best evidenced in the Ncf1m1J mouse where diminished ROS leads to exacerbated inflammation in arthritis and lupus models.
source: The protective effects of ROS against autoimmune diseases in vivo are best evidenced in the Ncf1m1J mouse where diminished ROS leads to exacerbated inflammation in arthritis and lupus models (Olofsson et al., 2003; Kelkka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: NOX2 is expressed in antigen-presenting cells and can upon antigen presentation expose T cells to hydrogen peroxide.
source: NOX2 is expressed in antigen-presenting cells and can upon antigen presentation expose T cells to hydrogen peroxide, that is, ROS (Gelderman et al., 2006; Gelderman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: ROS exposure regulates NFAT activation, IL2 production, and plasticity by both influencing the redox status of kinases involved and through metabolic reprogramming.
source: This ROS exposure regulates NFAT activation, IL2 production, and plasticity by both influencing the redox status of kinases involved and through metabolic reprogramming (Kesarwani et al., 2013; Contento et al., 2010; Gelderman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Reversible cysteine modifications have emerged as a major redox regulatory mechanism important for ERK1/2 phosphorylation, calcium flux, cell growth, and proliferation of naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Reversible cysteine modifications have emerged as a major redox regulatory mechanism important for ERK1/2 phosphorylation, calcium flux, cell growth, and proliferation of naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (García-Santamarina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Proteins containing cysteine residues, such as PTPs, are particularly susceptible to redox effects in part due to the low pKa value of their active site.
source: Proteins containing cysteine residues, such as PTPs, are particularly susceptible to redox effects in part due to the low pKa value of their active site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: Oxidation leads to inhibition of PTP activity.
source: Oxidation leads to inhibition of PTP activity, and several PTPs such as Src homology region 2 domain-containing phosphatase-1 and 2 (SHP1/2) and tyrosine-protein phosphatase non-receptor type 1 (PTP1B) are well studied in terms of their redox regulation (Ostman et al., 2011; Michalek et al., 2007; Frijhoff et al., 2014; Tonks, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The thioredoxin system is important for its reductive PTP-activating capacity.
source: The thioredoxin system is important for its reductive PTP-activating capacity (Dagnell et al., 2013; Dóka et al., 2020; Dagnell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: PTPN22 is a PTP expressed in all hematopoietic cells and a known negative regulator of T cell signaling.
source: PTPN22 is a PTP expressed in all hematopoietic cells and a known negative regulator of T cell signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: The R620W variant of PTPN22 has been associated with an increased risk of several autoimmune diseases, amongst them diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
source: The R620W variant of PTPN22 has been associated with an increased risk of several autoimmune diseases, amongst them diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.

claim: The R620W variant has been shown to interfere with the binding of PTPN22 to the C-terminal SRC kinase (CSK) affecting downstream signaling.
source: It has been shown to interfere with the binding of PTPN22 to the C-terminal SRC kinase (CSK) affecting downstream signaling.

claim: A possibility for redox regulation of PTPN22 was highlighted by Tsai et al., who discovered an atypical disulfide bond formation between the catalytic cysteine C227 and a 'back-door' cysteine C129, as visualized in a crystal structure of the catalytic domain of PTPN22.
source: A possibility for redox regulation of PTPN22 was highlighted by Tsai et al., who discovered an atypical disulfide bond formation between the catalytic cysteine C227 and a 'back-door' cysteine C129, as visualized in a crystal structure of the catalytic domain of PTPN22 (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The reason behind the initial decrease in activity of PTPN22C129S remains to be studied.
source: The reason behind the initial decrease in activity remains to be studied; the single cysteine-to-serine change may affect the PTPN22 protein conformation or dynamics and crystallography studies would be needed to address this.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an area for future research.

claim: The pure PTPN22C129S migrated slightly slower than wild-type PTPN22, despite the only difference between the two proteins being the single C129 residue.
source: It should also be noted that the pure PTPN22C129S migrated slightly slower than wild-type PTPN22, despite the only difference between the two proteins being the single C129 residue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The disulfide bond that can be formed between C227 and C129 protects the catalytic C227 residue from overoxidation to sulphinic or sulphonic acid.
source: Based on our findings, we propose a model for the redox regulation of PTPN22, with the disulfide bond that can be formed between C227 and C129 protecting the catalytic C227 residue from overoxidation to sulphinic or sulphonic acid.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: It is possible that an alternative sulphenylamide motif can be made between the thiol group of the C227 with the peptide bond amine, which can also be reduced by the thioredoxin system, similar to that seen with PTP1B.
source: It is also possible that an alternative sulphenylamide motif can be made between the thiol group of the C227 with the peptide bond amine, which can also be reduced by the thioredoxin system, similar to that seen with PTP1B (Dagnell et al., 2013; Schwertassek et al., 2014) even if that motif was not seen in the crystal structure of PTPN22 (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possibility, with citations to support the mechanism in PTP1B.

source: In T cells, the PTPN22C129S mutation led to enhanced T cell activation and proliferation.

source: The PTPN22 targets LCK, Fyn, and Zap70 showed increased phosphorylation, arguing for lower catalytic activity of PTPN22C129S in vivo and confirming our in vitro findings.

source: In TCR signaling, phosphorylation of PKC-θ is a late-stage event that leads to the activation of transcription factors Nf-Kb, NFAT, and AP-1 controlling T cell functions down the line (Wang et al., 2012).

source: We observed baseline upregulation of p-PKC-θ in PTPN22C129S T cells, which did not respond to further TCR stimulation.

source: PKC phosphorylation is regulated by germinal center kinase-like kinase (GLK) and LCK (Wang et al., 2012; Brezar et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2008).

source: An increase in LCK phosphorylation as previously observed might therefore be causing increased p-PKC-θ.

source: This might be mediated by direct effects of ROS on PKC as it contains several redox-sensitive residues that can lead to PKC inactivation (Steinberg, 2015).

source: Interestingly, in the Ptpn22 mutant, we observed downregulation of CENPF, a cell cycle protein that was shown to be upregulated upon TrxR inhibition (Selenius et al., 2012).

source: Enhanced T cell activation led to increased inflammation in vivo, and we observed a pronounced skewing towards Th1 responses.

claim: A link between PTPN22 and Th1 responses has previously been established; PTPN22-/- and PTPN22R619W mice accumulate Th1 effector cells in their lymphoid organs with age or upon immune challenge.
source: A link between PTPN22 and Th1 responses has previously been established; PTPN22-/- and PTPN22R619W mice accumulate Th1 effector cells in their lymphoid organs with age or upon immune challenge.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: Th1 expansion in PTPN22-/- and PTPN22R619W mice was found to be dependent on LFA-ICAM1 interactions.
source: Th1 expansion in these mice was found to be dependent on LFA-ICAM1 interactions (Sanchez-Blanco et al., 2018).

claim: A collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model produced no visible differences in inflammation in PTPN22C129S mice.
source: A collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model produced no visible differences in inflammation in PTPN22C129S mice, in line with previous data showing that even a complete lack of PTPN22 does not result in significant differences in inflammation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Sanchez-Blanco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: An explanation for the lack of difference in CIA could be that the major pathogenic factor in the CIA model are autoreactive B cells producing pathogenic antibodies, rather than autoreactive T cells.
source: An explanation could be that the major pathogenic factor in the CIA model are autoreactive B cells producing pathogenic antibodies, rather than autoreactive T cells (Holmdahl et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In both T-cell-mediated inflammatory models (DTH and GPI) as well as on the Col2-T cell transgenic background, PTPN22C129S mice displayed higher T cell activity as well as more regulatory T cell markers such as FOXP3 and PD1.
source: In both T-cell-mediated inflammatory models (DTH and GPI) as well as on the Col2-T cell transgenic background, PTPN22C129S mice displayed higher T cell activity as well as more regulatory T cell markers such as FOXP3 and PD1 (shown for GPI model).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: A rise in Treg numbers is a measure to combat inflammation.
source: A rise in Treg numbers is a measure to combat inflammation, but where they originate from is a matter of discussion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: Tregs can originate from the thymus and migrate to the tissue in response to inflammation or result from conversion of CD4+ CD25- naïve T cells in the periphery.
source: They can originate from the thymus and migrate to the tissue in response to inflammation or result from conversion of CD4+ CD25- naïve T cells in the periphery (Yadav et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: PTPN22 plays an important role in determining TCR signal strength during central tolerance.
source: PTPN22 plays an important role in determining TCR signal strength during central tolerance; PTPN22-deficient mice show increased positive selection in the thymus as well as increased Treg numbers both in the thymus and periphery, leading to protection from the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model of autoimmunity (Maine et al., 2012; Hasegawa et al., 2004; Fousteri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Treg numbers were comparable between wild-type and PTPN22C129S thymi, suggesting peripheral induction of Tregs upon inflammation in PTPN22C129S mice.
source: In our study, Treg numbers were comparable between wild-type and PTPN22C129S thymi, suggesting peripheral induction of Tregs upon inflammation in PTPN22C129S mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The peripheral induction of Tregs may be a consequence of increased IFNɣ production by PTPN22C129S T cells as studies have also associated FOXP3 induction to Th1 responses.
source: This may be a consequence of increased IFNɣ production by PTPN22C129S T cells as studies have also associated FOXP3 induction to Th1 responses; this mechanism links IFNɣ and IL27 with amplifying TGF-b-induced FOXP3 expression via STAT1 (Ouaked et al., 2009; Littringer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation, with citations to support the mechanism.

claim: Previous studies have shown the essential role of PKC-θ in NFAT-dependent FOXP3 expression.
source: Previous studies have also shown the essential role of PKC-θ in NFAT-dependent FOXP3 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as background information.

claim: PKC-θ−/− mice have significantly reduced CD4+ FOXP3+ Tregs in the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes.
source: PKC-θ−/− mice have significantly reduced CD4+ FOXP3+ Tregs in the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes (Gupta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The rise in Tregs in PTPN22C129S mice may be a consequence of the enhanced baseline PKC-θ signaling.
source: Accordingly, the rise in Tregs in PTPN22C129S mice may be a consequence of the enhanced baseline PKC-θ signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The activity of PTPN22 can be regulated by ROS through its noncatalytic C129 residue, which is likely to have a major impact on its function in addition to that of merely altered basal turnover.
source: In summary, our results show how the activity of PTPN22, a gene where a risk variant is associated with autoimmune diseases, can be regulated by ROS through its noncatalytic C129 residue, which is likely to have a major impact on its function in addition to that of merely altered basal turnover (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: It has been notoriously difficult to target PTPs in vivo with drug therapies due to the nature of their active sites.
source: It has been notoriously difficult to target PTPs in vivo with drug therapies due to the nature of their active sites (Stanford and Bottini, 2017), but recent advances in targeting the redox status of T lymphocytes might represent a novel strategy to treat T-cell-driven diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Antibody-trapping of the oxidized form of PTP1B has been shown to increase insulin signaling in vitro.
source: Antibody-trapping of the oxidized form of PTP1B, a highly touted drug target for diabetes and obesity, has been shown to increase insulin signaling in vitro (Stanford and Bottini, 2014; Krishnan et al., 2018; Stanford and Bottini, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.
